Why Darkstar exists

Build robots. Not another broken development environment.

A native Mac experience for Linux-first robotics development. Darkstar aims to help MacBook users get from incompatible dependencies and VM troubleshooting to meaningful robotics experiments—with transparent diagnostics and reproducible results.

Mac-native experience

Keep the portable MacBook workflow you enjoy while using Linux tools where the robotics stack requires them.

Compatibility before installation

Choose documented Ubuntu, ROS 2, Gazebo, and PX4 combinations instead of discovering version mismatches the hard way.

Diagnose the environment

Expose prerequisite, virtual graphics, and runtime issues with understandable next steps—not silent, irreversible configuration changes.

From the builder

Why I built it.

I love the portability and thoughtful design of MacBooks. But when I started working with ROS 2, PX4, and Gazebo, I spent too much time wrestling with virtual machines, setup instructions, dependency combinations, and graphics problems. At one point a browser inside my Linux VM stopped working until I changed a Wayland-related session setting. I wanted to build the Mac-native gateway to Linux robotics development I wish I'd had when I started.

This isn't about replacing Linux or claiming macOS cannot run robotics software. It's about making supported workflows easier to find, configure, troubleshoot, and verify—so students and independent builders can spend more time learning and building.

Architecture

Modular, not monolithic.

Darkstar Robotics is not an all-or-nothing installation. Nobody should have to install ROS 2, Gazebo, PX4, Docker, and dozens of other tools just to open the application. You start with the Core — everything else is opt-in.

“Darkstar Robotics Core must remain independently usable. Robotics applications, runtimes, SDKs, and hardware integrations are opt-in. Readiness is evaluated against the user's selected capabilities, not the entire software catalog.”

Product principle — Phase 1 spec

Layer 1

Core

The lightweight desktop application: system inspector, compatibility engine, application catalog, and diagnostics interface. No ROS, Gazebo, PX4, or simulator installation required to start.

Required — that's all
Layer 2

Optional Applications

Choose individual tools only when you need them — ROS 2, Gazebo, PlatformIO, OpenCV, QGroundControl, KiCad. Want only QGroundControl? Nothing forces ROS 2 or Gazebo along with it. Building for an ESP32? PX4 stays out of it.

Opt-in · per tool
Layer 3

Optional Stacks

Curated combinations for drone development, rovers, robot arms, embedded systems, and computer vision. Every component is individually selectable — a stack is a starting point, never an all-or-nothing bundle.

Proposed — not validated

Dependencies, in the open

A selected tool may need other software to work. Darkstar Robotics explains those dependencies and asks for approval — it never installs anything silently. Every dependency in the catalog is one of three types:

Required

Must be present for the selected capability to work at all. If it's missing, that capability — and only that capability — reports it.

Optional

Adds functionality, but the selected capability works without it. An absent optional dependency is never an error.

Alternative

A choice between supported implementations. Pick the one your workflow already uses; the catalog tracks either.

Two kinds of readiness

Workstation readiness

Is Darkstar Robotics itself functioning correctly — the Core application, its system inspector, and its diagnostics?

Measured against the Core only

Stack readiness

Does this machine meet the requirements of the specific tools and workflow you selected — and only the ones you selected?

Measured against your selection

Never selected PX4? Its absence is not an error and raises no dashboard warning. It simply reads Not Installed in the catalog — neutral, until the day you choose it.

Download

Get the installer.

Darkstar Robotics v0.4.0 is out — tonight's fixes, properly packaged, with a real app icon and a valid ad-hoc signature. One honest wrinkle: the build isn't notarized by Apple, so on first open macOS will say it "could not verify" the installer — that's Gatekeeper doing its job on any non-notarized app, not a broken download. Dismiss the dialog, then go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway. It's a one-time step; after that the installer walks the app into place — logo, status check, and all.

Darkstar Robotics Installer

The installer GUI checks for an existing install, shows what it found, and installs Darkstar Robotics to your Applications folder in one click. Prefer to skip the installer? The app-only zip is the same build, ready to drag in yourself.

New in v0.4.0: the validated application catalog and the Omega-Ubuntu theme ship in the tree, error handling is typed end to end, and the installer is transactional — a failed install rolls back cleanly instead of leaving a half-copied app behind.

Get it

Open Xcode. Press run.

The source is public and the workstation is in active development. Clone the repository, inspect the requirements, and run the current build.

Terminal — zsh
# Clone Darkstar Robotics
$ git clone https://github.com/abelxmendoza/HangarBay.git
$ cd HangarBay

# Run it — or just open Package.swift in Xcode
$ swift run

# Settings (⌘,) holds the VM name + SSH target.
# → Dashboard live. Runtime probing…
  • macOS 14+ — Sonoma or laterHOST
  • Xcode — open Package.swift and press RunTOOLCHAIN
  • UTM — hosts the managed Linux runtimeRUNTIME
  • Tailscale — the link between GUI and guestLINK
  • Internal name — the Swift package is still RoboticsControlCenter; the product is Darkstar RoboticsNOTE
